query: When should firms prefer expectation-based planning versus CVaR/LOLP for site-dependent failures, and how to translate these metrics into capacity expansion and cost decisions?

response.query: When should firms prefer expectation-based planning versus CVaR/LOLP for site-dependent failures, and how to translate these metrics into capacity expansion and cost decisions?
response.answer: Firms prefer expectation-based planning for short-term, predictable scenarios; CVaR/LOLP for site-dependent failures in long-term, uncertain conditions. These metrics guide capacity expansion by balancing investment costs against reliability risks.

results.title: Capacity Expansion as a Strategic Decision
results.content: # Capacity Expansion as a Strategic Decision. "Capacity expansion is one of the most significant strategic decisions faced by firms, measured both in terms of the amount of capital involved and the complexity of the decision-making problem." - Michael Porter (Author of Competitive Strategy). Given the high-level of fragmentation in the construction industry, along with the wide range of scale and outcomes between contractors, it is obvious that neither strategy nor execution is a commodity in the industry. The best thing you can do as a leader within a construction company is study the growing body of knowledge around strategy and execution. Then make the best strategic decisions you can and follow through with deliberate execution. Chapter 15 dives into the strategic decisions associated with capacity expansion and is well worth reading. Capacity expansion is one of the most significant strategic decisions faced by firms, measured both in terms of the amount of capital involved and the complexity of the decision-making problem. Because capacity additions can involve lead times measured in years and capacity is often long lasting, capacity decisions require the firm to commit resources based on expectations about conditions far into the future. The importance of the former in capacity decisions is obvious. Thus, capacity expansion involves all the classic problems of oligopoly, in which firms are mutually dependent. The strategic issue in capacity expansion is how to add capacity to further the objectives of the firm, in the hope of improving its competitive position or market share, while avoiding industry overcapacity. Under capacity in an industry is rarely a problem, except temporarily, since it will usually attract new investment. This chapter will explore the capacity expansion decision in a strategic context. Finally, the preemptive strategy for capacity expansion will be discussed. 1. Will greater scale make us more competitive given our strategic market choices? Improve the quality and quantity of projects you win with these 10 questions to evaluate your strategic market choices and the progress on executing that strategy. ##### Tactical and Strategic Question Categories. When planning, separate the questions you ask yourself into tactical and strategic categories. ##### Alignment from Strategy to Execution.

results.title: Limitations of the Loss of Load Probability/Expectation Criterion in Electric Power Systems
results.content: Recent U.S. blackouts in Texas and California and many international blackouts are leading many to reconsider the reliability and resiliency policies of the electric power system. One element that is being discussed is whether the loss of load probability (LOLP) or loss of load expectation (LOLE) criterion of “one-day-in-ten-years” or “one-time-in-ten-years” should be replaced, perhaps by an expected unserved energy criterion or set of other reliability metrics. The deficiencies with the LOLP/LOLE criterion are well known and were raised many years ago, including noting that this criterion does not account for the magnitude of power outages. For example, not considering emergency generation ratings during capacity shortages makes it more difficult for a generation system to meet the one-day-in-10- years criterion than does considering these emergency ratings. *A third limitation of the LOLP criterion is that it is not a useful index of widespread blackouts. For example, assume that the LOLP is 0.1 and the average amount of the load curtailment is 100 MW out of a 20,000 MW system.

results.title: (PDF) Capacity Expansion Planning under Uncertainty subject to Expected Energy Not Served Constraints
results.content: We present a method for solving a large-scale stochastic capacity expansion problem which explicitly considers reliability constraints, in particular constraints on expected energy not served. Each iteration requires the solution of a stochastic capacity expansion problem, for which we implement a subgradient decomposition scheme in a high-performance computing infrastructure. The case of explicit reliability constraints corresponds to the results of the proposed algorithm, while the implicit case corresponds to results obtained from a single run of the algorithm for a uniform λ of 15 000 EUR/MWh for all bidding zones. solve a least-cost capacity expansion problem satisfying EENS, as well as CVaR. Overall, the stochastic capacity expansion model with EENS constraints is for-. plan and solve the CEP-EENS-R problem to obtain its true cost. beneﬁt of allowing some load shedding in the capacity planning process, e.g. in the case study analyzed allowing for load shedding consistent to the ERAA. pt,n,g,ω : generation by existing capacities (MW). t,n,g,ω : generation by new capacities (MW). Our work formulates the problem as a two-stage stochastic problem and proposes two decomposition algorithms for solving the problem which are implemented in a high-performance computing infrastructure. This work presents a methodology to incorporate reliability constraints in the optimal power systems expansion planning problem. The explicit consideration of reliability constraints in the planning problem can be an extremely hard task and, to minimize computational effort, this work applies the Benders decomposition technique splitting the expansion planning problem into an investment problem and two subproblems to evaluate the system's operation cost and the reliability index. This paper presents a tri-level reliability-constrained robust power system expansion planning (SEP) framework modeling the uncertainty of electricity demand, wind power generation, and availability of units and lines. This paper describes a new probabilistic model for generation and transmission expansion planning (G&TEP) problem considering reliability criteria. The resultant model considers the installation and operation costs as well as the cost of expected energy not supplied (EENS) to optimally determine the number and location of new generating units and circuits in the network, power generation capacity for those units and the voltage phase angle at each node.

results.title: Capacity Versus Expectation
results.content:
Title: Capacity Versus Expectation
# Capacity Versus Expectation. I have shared this Neuro Success ™ strategy with hundreds over the years. I hope it brings understanding and breakthrough to you too, or someone you share it with. Expectations are an interesting bunch: they have the power to either support or totally sabotage our success. Allow me to explain…   Capacity Versus ExpectationLet’s say people’s capacity, i.e., all their humanly possible behaviours, sit within the circle. Our expectations are represented by an “X”. When we place our expectations of a person within their capacity, they are able to be met. Capacity Versus ExpectationThe challenge is when we place our expectations of a person’s behaviour outside of their capacity! Here’s the super important part: What you think (***or expect of***) a person’s capacity *should* be, may not be what it *actually* is at that given moment! That’s simply **your** expectations placed upon them. Super important part 2: **CAPACITY IS FLUID**. At any given moment, capacity can change, either expanding or shrinking. BUT I will have still given 100 percent of my capacity for that day. You, therefore, would have exactly the same capacity as them and you would have done exactly what they did, because that’s all you would be capable of!” For many years, I placed expectations on people outside of their capacity. I was constantly disappointed and frustrated because my expectations were unmet. It wasn’t until I had an epiphany of capacity and expectation that it allowed me to see that these individuals had given 100 percent of what they had. I may have wanted more but it was unreasonable of me to expect them to give more than what they had. In time, their capacity may grow and they may be able to give more; but for now, I choose to be grateful that they have honoured me by giving 100 percent of what they had. This revelation grew my capacity. #### Share This. Simone Leslie is a Master Neuro Strategist, speaker, author & blogger for Her Business, (formerly the Australian Business Women’s Network.)  Over the past two decades she has presented to millions through national television and live audiences.
